newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. troop cut could spark Asia arms race -- Cohen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. troop cut could spark Asia arms race -- Cohen.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen warned on Tuesday that any reduction of American troop numbers in the Western Pacific could trigger a dangerous arms race in Asia.

He stressed that the 100,000 U.S. troops in the region, most of them in Japan and South Korea, were not aimed at containing China and that their full stabilising presence should continue even if North and South Korea reunify.
"It is not designed against China at all, but to maintain stability in the region," Cohen told reporters during a visit to Japan.
"Whatever China does in terms of the future, it is not really going to alter what I believe is a sound policy for having a presence in the region. It is a very large region."
He said that even a partial U.S. withdrawal would frighten American allies and could trigger a dangerous arms race to fill a power vacuum.

"If we were to have a substantial reduction of our force in the region, I believe that would set up a very negative dynamic, namely other countries would then feel an obligation to start arming themselves to a much higher level than they currently are," he added.
"That would not bode well for the region. It might, in fact, contribute to greater potential for conflict, which is something we do not want."
There are 47,000 U.S. troops in Japan and another 36,000 in South Korea.
Cohen told reporters travelling with him at the weekend that he did not believe the troop level in Korea should be reduced over the short term, even if peace comes to the peninsula.

He added on Tuesday that the situation in heavily armed and Stalinist North Korea was very unstable and that the United States was having a difficult time assessing the extent of hunger reported in the North.
He denied, however, that the United States was using food as a weapon by its cautious response to reports of near-famine conditions in North Korea.
"Our policy is not to either feed fat generals or to starve innocent people, but rather to be of help where humanitarian assistance can be helpful," Cohen said.
He stressed the United States would provide food aid to Pyongyang only in consultation with South Korea and Japan.
"We are told that there is real hardship," he said. "Whether that is going to ameliorate the policies of the North or harden the policies of the North remains to be seen."

Cohen on Tuesday also repeated his call for South Korea to reject an offer from Russia to sell SA-12 anti-aircraft missiles to Seoul, noting again that they could accidentally threaten U.S. aircraft in any new Korean conflict because of electronic differences with American equipment.
Cohen has called on ally South Korea to instead buy Patriot air defence missiles made by Raytheon Corp.

Asked by a reporter why the United States was objecting to the SA-12s when the South Koreans were already buying French-made anti-aircraft missiles without equipment to identify friendly warplanes, he bridled.
"I don't see that you gain anything by compounding a problem, by encouraging others to add to a problem that may already exist," he said.

"I would encourage the South Koreans to buy American Patriots as opposed to either French-made or Russian-made (missiles)," he said, pouring fuel on a controversy set off in South Korea by his earlier comments.
"I think that the Koreans would be well-served by having American equipment, period."
